strengths: Novel combination addressing a genuine gap: First foundation model explicitly combining macro- and micro-structure sleep analysis with clinical motivation
Well-motivated DGCL objective: Demographic-guided contrastive learning for macro-structure is innovative and empirically justified with clear demographic patterns (Figure 4)
Large-scale pretraining dataset: 20,964 PSG recordings across 7 datasets (158K hours) with comprehensive documentation enables meaningful pretrained representations

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple downstream tasks (staging, segmentation, disease prediction), datasets (SHHS1, KISS, ISRUC), proper ablations (Tables 11-12) demonstrating component contributions
Impressive few-shot learning: Achieving 72.6% accuracy with only 30 training samples (2.1% below full-dataset performance) demonstrates practical label efficiency
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, architecture specifications, preprocessing, and dataset statistics enable reproduction; honest limitations discussion
Strong embedding analysis: Figures 6 and 10 convincingly demonstrate that DGCL successfully captures and organizes demographic information in learned representations
weaknesses: Hardware generalization failure: MOMENT outperforms SleepMaMi on KISS dataset (69.8% vs 62.8%), attributed to model benefiting from Compumedics hardware dominance in pretraining. This undermines 'universal' foundation model claims and raises concerns about deployment across different PSG systems

Disease prediction results only comparable, not superior: Table 3 shows mixed/worse performance on 3/6 diseases vs. SleepFM-Disease (Angina, MI, Stroke), contradicting central motivation that dual-encoder design improves health prediction

Weak and suboptimal baselines: Time-series FMs perform surprisingly poorly (UniTS: 60.3% on KISS sleep staging), suggesting unfair comparison. Missing comparisons with recent specialized sleep models (SleepTransformer, U-Sleep) that achieve ~85% on SHHS1

Limited technical novelty: Individual components (Transformers, Mamba, MAE, CL) are well-established. Novelty is primarily in application/combination rather than new methods. DGCL is straightforward demographic-distance application to contrastive learning

Unvalidated DGCL assumptions: Model assumes demographic similarity implies sleep macro-structure similarity, but this may not hold for individuals with sleep disorders (primary clinical use case). No analysis of assumption validity or performance on underrepresented populations

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. No cross-dataset evaluation (train on SHHS1, test on KISS). Small test sets for ISRUC (n=10-16). Single random seed/split not explicitly stated

Incomplete architectural justification: Only 2 Mamba layers for 800+ epoch sequences seems shallow. 90-minute cycle choice arbitrary for fragmented sleep. Masking strategy (500ms/2s) lacks principled justification. No sensitivity analysis for temperature parameters (τ, ρ, υ)
Potential demographic bias: DGCL uses age/BMI/sex as supervisory signals without discussing how this encodes/reinforces healthcare disparities or performs across demographic groups

Code availability and reproducibility gaps: Pretrained models not released; code only mentioned as 'PyTorch'. High computational requirements (2×H100 GPUs, 10 hours) limit reproducibility. Some dataset access restricted

strengths: Large-scale pretraining on comprehensive, well-documented PSG dataset (20,964 recordings)
Technically sophisticated dual-encoder architecture with thoughtful design choices (Mamba for efficiency, MoE, hierarchical merging)
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple downstream tasks with proper protocols (linear probing, class imbalance handling)
Detailed reproducibility information in extensive appendices with hyperparameters and implementation details
Clear motivation for joint modeling of micro and macro-structure with clinical justification
weaknesses: Critical hardware distribution shift: 19% accuracy degradation on KISS (62.8%) vs SHHS1 (81.9%), and worse than MOMENT baseline on KISS—directly contradicts 'universal' foundation model claims with only vague explanation about sensor-agnostic trade-offs

Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) contribution poorly justified: (1) no principled explanation why demographic metadata should guide sleep architecture learning, (2) marginal empirical benefit (~1% in ablation Table 12), (3) potential demographic bias risk for clinical applications

Disease prediction results do not support superiority claims: Table 3 shows only comparable performance to SleepFM-Disease with mixed results (inferior on Stroke), contradicting abstract's claim of 'outperforms existing foundation models'

Weak baseline comparisons: MOMENT/UniTS are general time-series models not designed for PSG (strawman comparisons), missing comparisons against other sleep-specific models cited in related work (U-Sleep, XSleepNet, SleepTransformer)

Micro-Encoder complexity underanalyzed: hierarchical patch merging and private-shared architecture add complexity but ablation shows minimal improvement (~1-2%), with unclear necessity vs. simpler alternatives

Limited statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple runs reported; few-shot evaluation only on ISRUC (small, different distribution) rather than SHHS1/KISS; potential data leakage with SHHS1 train split used for DGCL pretraining and downstream evaluation

Marginal overall improvements: Table 4 shows Macro-Encoder adds ~2% to sleep staging but ablation doesn't clearly show whether this is from DGCL or just additional pretraining; few-shot results don't strongly differentiate encoder contributions

Overstated 'universal' framing: acknowledged poor cross-hardware generalization, hardware-specific overfitting, lack of domain adaptation strategies, and limited analysis of failure modes undermine the central 'universal' foundation model claim

strengths: Addresses clinically important problem with clear motivation for integrating micro and macro-structure in sleep analysis
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and diverse downstream tasks (staging, segmentation, disease prediction) with thorough ablations
Large-scale pretraining on 20,964 PSG recordings with careful documentation of preprocessing, datasets, and hyperparameters enabling reproducibility

Technically sound dual-encoder architecture with well-motivated design choices: patch-merging for efficiency, Mamba for long-sequence modeling, and DGCL leveraging objective metadata to avoid annotation noise
Strong empirical results generally outperforming baselines, especially on fine-grained SDB segmentation (macro-F1 improvements of 21.2% on SHHS1, 10.3% on KISS)
Excellent visualization and analysis of learned representations showing clear demographic clustering and clinically relevant macro-structure patterns
Honest acknowledgment and discussion of hardware distribution shift limitations affecting KISS dataset performance
weaknesses: Hardware distribution shift undermines universality claims: model trained predominantly on Compumedics systems shows substantially worse performance on Nox/Embla systems (KISS: 62.8% vs MOMENT's 69.8%), indicating overfitting to specific hardware characteristics rather than learning generalizable sleep features

Limited true cross-dataset generalization: most evaluations use test sets from same dataset as training; critical cross-dataset evaluation (train on SHHS1, test on KISS) is missing, which is essential for foundation model validation

Marginal or inconsistent improvements on key clinical task of disease prediction: results are comparable to rather than clearly superior to SleepFM-Disease, with mixed results across diseases (improved on Angina/MI but worse on Stroke/CHF)

Confounding between demographic information and macro-structure: demographics (age, sex, BMI) directly influence sleep architecture; DGCL embeds demographic information in pretraining, making it unclear whether improvements stem from learning sleep structure or demographic encoding; downstream tasks include demographic prediction exacerbating this concern

DGCL design choices lack rigorous justification: demographic distance formula (Eq. 5) appears ad-hoc with arbitrary equal weighting and fixed penalties; ablation (Table 12) shows modest gains (79.8%→80.7%) from demographics; insufficient analysis of what macro-structure features are learned independent of demographics

Limited novelty in individual components: MAE and contrastive learning are established, Mamba is increasingly standard; primary novelty in DGCL is relatively straightforward application of soft-target contrastive learning with demographic distance as supervisory signal

Incomplete analysis of learned representations: while Figure 6 shows demographic clustering, lacks analysis of whether embeddings capture clinically meaningful sleep patterns independent of demographics or which micro-structure features the model prioritizes

Two-stage sequential pretraining (Micro→Macro) is suboptimal; joint training merits exploration but not evaluated; no sensitivity analysis for architectural choices (MoE experts, patch sizes, merge strategy)

strengths: Well-motivated unified framework explicitly combining micro and macro sleep structures, addressing a genuine gap in existing models
Thoughtful architectural design with bi-directional Mamba for efficiency and private-shared encoders for multi-modal heterogeneity
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse downstream tasks (4 classification, 2 regression, disease prediction) with strong cross-dataset generalization to held-out datasets (CFS, SOF)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed architecture specifications, complete hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, comprehensive ablations (Tables 12-16), and promised code release
Impressive label efficiency demonstrated through few-shot learning (Figure 5), with competitive performance from single samples
Thoughtful treatment of fairness concerns with empirical demographic bias analysis (Table 11) and impact statement addressing ethical implications
weaknesses: Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) design is empirically ad-hoc: manual hyperparameter (λ_sex=1), lacks theoretical justification for why demographic similarity should organize representations, and raises unresolved ethical concerns about reinforcing clinical biases
Improvements over baselines are often modest, particularly for disease prediction where C-indices nearly match SleepFM (Table 3), limiting claims about clinical significance

Specialist models substantially outperform: SleePyCo achieves 87.9% vs 85.2% for sleep staging (Table 17) and AIX achieves 93.8% vs 77.3% for SDB (Table 19), raising questions about practical clinical adoption
Hierarchical masking strategy (Section 3.1) lacks clarity on temporal alignment preservation and information loss during hierarchical merging, with no direct ablation validating this design choice
Reconstruction loss applies signal smoothing (11-point moving average) only in appendix, potentially introducing artifacts for fine-grained features (spindles, K-complexes) without ablation
Critical lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; stability across random seeds not reported; single-run ablations

Limited clinical validation with disease prediction restricted to 6 outcomes on one dataset (SHHS1); no prospective validation or comparison to clinical standards despite claims of 'long-term prognostic prediction'
Notation inconsistencies and underspecified architectural details: Mixture of Experts routing mechanism not explained, cross-attention operations (Figure 2) lack implementation details

strengths: Addresses genuine gap: First explicit integration of sleep micro-structure and macro-structure in a unified foundation model, with clinically motivated motivation

Large-scale pretraining with strong generalization: 20,964 recordings across diverse datasets (SHHS, KISS, MESA, MrOS), evaluated on held-out cohorts (CFS, SOF) demonstrating genuine cross-dataset generalization
Sound architectural design: Private-shared encoder for multi-modal signals is principled; Mamba choice over Transformers justified by memory efficiency; hierarchical abstraction appropriate

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive ablation studies (Tables 12-16), few-shot learning curves, embedding visualizations, multiple downstream tasks (staging, segmentation, disease prediction)
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters (Appendix C), architectural specs (Appendix B), multiple public datasets used, claims code availability
weaknesses: Core innovation (DGCL) lacks rigorous validation: Demographic-guided pretraining is asserted to improve downstream clinical tasks, but causal mechanism is unclear. Table 13 shows diminishing returns (age alone: 80.6%, all three: 80.7%), and Table 4 shows modest gains (79.8%→81.9%), leaving unclear how much improvement comes from DGCL vs. larger training data alone

Critical ethical concerns inadequately addressed: Using demographic metadata to organize representation space risks encoding historical biases in sleep medicine. Appendix E's subgroup analysis is superficial; no fairness framework for clinical deployment; bias risks are acknowledged defensively rather than rigorously mitigated

Inconsistent improvements over most relevant baseline (SleepFM-Disease): Disease prediction shows mixed results (Stroke: 0.729→0.718 regression), and specialized models outperform (Table 19: AIX 93.8% vs. SleepMaMi 77.3% on SDB segmentation). Unfair comparisons to general time-series models (MOMENT, UniTS) don't validate clinical innovation

Presentation density and arbitrary design choices: Figure 2 is visually complex; hierarchical merging mechanism lacks intuitive explanation. Arbitrary decisions unexplored: why different masking for high/low frequencies? Why universal 90-minute cycles? How handled for <90-min recordings? Why two-stage training?

Limited fundamental novelty: MAE, contrastive learning, Transformer/Mamba architectures, and multi-task pretraining are established. DGCL is straightforward application of weighted InfoNCE to demographics. Contribution is primarily in combination/application rather than methodological innovation

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation explicitly integrating macro- and micro-structures of sleep, addressing a genuine gap in sleep medicine where prior work focused on one or the other

Thoughtful dual-encoder architecture with private-shared encoders for micro-structures and bi-directional Mamba for macro-structures, with careful attention to computational efficiency and variable sequence lengths

DGCL (Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning) is a clever innovation that leverages objective metadata to circumvent inter-scorer variability and manual annotation burden without requiring subjective labels

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse downstream tasks (sleep staging, SDB segmentation, disease prediction, age/sex/AHI estimation) with multiple held-out test datasets demonstrating strong generalization
Impressive label-efficient adaptation with few-shot learning results (44.1% F1 with 1 sample → 71.8% with 30 samples), valuable for clinical applications with limited labeled data
Extensive reproducibility support including detailed hyperparameters, model architectures, preprocessing specifications, and promised code/checkpoints release
Large-scale pretraining on 20,964 PSG recordings (158K hours) provides valuable resource for the community
weaknesses: Disease prediction results (Table 3) show only comparable performance to SleepFM-Disease, not clear improvements, which undermines the stated motivation for macro-structure modeling as 'vital biomarker for long-term health outcomes'

DGCL's use of demographic metadata as soft supervision poses ethical risks of encoding historical biases; while subgroup analysis is provided, fairness evaluation is incomplete and potential demographic shortcuts are not fully mitigated
Significant performance gap to specialized models on certain tasks (e.g., SDB segmentation: AIX 93.8% vs SleepMaMi 77.3%), with limited discussion of this accuracy-generalizability tradeoff

Limited technical novelty in individual components (private-shared encoders, MAE+contrastive hybrid, Mamba); primary novelty is in problem formulation and DGCL rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation
Two-stage training of Micro and Macro encoders without justification or ablation for joint training; potential information loss between stages unexplored

Architectural design choices under-justified: 90-minute cycle length shows negligible variation (Table 14: 80.3-80.7%), demographic distance formula is hand-crafted with no comparison to learnable alternatives, and DGCL only marginally outperforms SimCLR/DINO (81.9% vs 81.8%/81.7%)

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported; limited error analysis or failure case discussion; linear probing may not fully utilize learned representations despite alternative LSTM evaluation in appendix
